clue.text: Stop (for 6?) to give a hand with hock joint preparation?

parts.note: to give someone a hand is to applaud, to clap
a hock is the joint of a pig's leg, cured as ham
J is slang shorthand for a joint, a cannabis cigarette
an unction is an ointment, a medical preparation for anointing

explanation.surface: A butcher's lesson on preparing a ham hock, with someone asked to lend a hand.
explanation.walkthrough: '(for 6?)' points to 6-down: a stop for the trains running up to London. CLAPHAM JUNCTION is a famously busy railway station in south London.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway junction station is a place where trains halt, so it is a stop for them.

clue.text: Inversely, almae maters like St Hilda's now, but not St Trinian's!

definitions.text: like St Hilda's now, but not St Trinian's

indicators.note: inversely says the two parts of the phrase swap places, front part going to the back

parts.note: an alma mater is one's former university, so these are ex-unis

explanation.surface: A comparison of an Oxford college with the fictional girls' school of St Trinian's.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the halves of EX-UNIS gives UNISEX. St Hilda's, Oxford, was the last women-only college and now admits men; St Trinian's is the riotous fictional girls' school of cartoons and films.
explanation.definitionFit: A college open to both men and women is mixed, which a girls-only school is not.

clue.text: Take off pair of stone fragments; replace with hard, black pipe

indicators.note: replace with says the letter dropped gives way to the next letter named, here a second swap
take off reads as a command to strip something away, here the R that stands for 'take'
a pair of means the piece is written down twice

parts.note: rubble is broken fragments of stone
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: Instructions for clearing rubble and swapping in a hard black pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: R is the abbreviation for Latin recipe, 'take', so 'Take off' removes an R from each RUBBLE; H replaces one and B the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A hubble-bubble is a hookah, a water pipe for smoking tobacco.

clue.text: Having intermittent doses of X-ray radiation finally prepared Ellington for one drink

indicators.note: intermittent doses means letters are dropped in here and there, scattered through the main piece
prepared means made ready, the dosing letters being put in a new arrangement

parts.note: Duke Ellington was a famous jazz band leader
taken as written

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of radiation

explanation.surface: A patient getting X-ray treatment while the Duke is made a cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: BANDLEADER keeps its order; the letters of X-RAY plus N, the last letter of 'radiation', are mixed up and slotted in at intervals: B(R)AND(Y)(A)LE(X)A(N)DER.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy alexander is a cocktail of brandy, crème de cacao and cream.

clue.text: Fun originally with Listener? Accepting failure, withdraw

indicators.note: accepting means taking something in, so one piece goes inside the other
the letters are shown in their original order, to be rearranged into a new form

parts.note: a no-no is informally a failure, something that will not work

explanation.surface: Someone tackling The Listener crossword for fun, failing, and giving up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listener' looks like a person but is The Listener, a famously hard British weekly crossword; a no-no is a dud, hence failure.
explanation.definitionFit: To retreat into one's own thoughts and become introverted is to withdraw socially.

clue.text: On the job, coaches shot out in a spurt

indicators.note: shot out suggests letters flung away and landing in a new order

explanation.surface: Sports coaches working in sudden bursts of activity.
explanation.definitionFit: Training staff up while they work is teaching them on the job, as a coach does.

clue.text: Open note — lets rip foully

indicators.note: foully means wickedly, but also in a fouled-up jumble of letters

explanation.surface: An unsealed message that unleashes a stream of vile abuse.
explanation.definitionFit: An anonymous malicious letter is unsealed abuse let loose, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Reluctant to hurry up the wall along our American borders

indicators.note: borders means lies beside, so one piece sits next to the other
up the wall means crazy, signalling the letters gone mad

parts.note: US stands for American, as in US citizen

explanation.surface: A wall along the American border that nobody is in a hurry to put up.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone languid and lazy is slow and listless, in no rush.

clue.text: Of popular vote, over a third for Australian PM

indicators.note: of says the letters come out of the phrase that follows
the run taken up is more than a third of the phrase's letters, four of eleven

explanation.surface: An Australian prime minister elected on more than a third of the popular vote.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Australian PM' looks like a prime minister; PM is post meridiem, the afternoon.
explanation.definitionFit: Arvo is Australian slang for afternoon, the hours abbreviated PM.

clue.text: Stepfathers, once separated?

definitions.meaning: a ballet step is called a ...
pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: Stepfathers who were once separated from their families.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once separated' tells you to split 'Stepfathers' into STEP and FATHERS, each giving the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: In ballet a pas is a dance step; pas is also the plural of the homely word for dads.

clue.text: Covers dispensed with to give more chances for slips?

definitions.text: Covers dispensed with to give more chances for slips?

parts.words: Covers dispensed with to give more chances for slips?
parts.note: the peel of a tropical fruit, once thrown away, is what people classically slip on; also a cricket-like hint of covers and slips

explanation.surface: A cricket captain removing his cover fielders to put more men in the slips.
explanation.walkthrough: Covers and slips are cricket fielding positions, which makes the surface look like a fielding change.
explanation.definitionFit: Discarded fruit peels cause literal falls, and figuratively mean pitfalls or blunders.

clue.text: Second go, in fear of what scanner will do

parts.note: to go is a slang euphemism for urinating, to pee
dreading something means being in fear of it

explanation.surface: A nervous patient going in for a second scan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scanner' looks like a medical machine but is a person scanning a text quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who scans a page skims it rapidly, gathering the gist at speed.

clue.text: Next, I negotiated in style with going concern

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside the other
going means leaving, so that letter departs from the word

parts.note: a way of doing things is a style

indicators.note: negotiated means worked out or got round, signalling the letters reworked

explanation.surface: A business deal negotiated stylishly with a firm that is a going concern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going concern' reads as a business phrase; 'going' acts on W, and 'concern' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Worry or unease about something is concern for it.

clue.text: Breaking news, one more Danish composer

indicators.note: breaking means splitting a piece open to let others in

parts.note: read as the plural of new, each abbreviated N, giving two Ns
I is the Roman numeral one
else means other or more, as in 'anything else'

explanation.surface: A breaking news story about one more Danish composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'news' is split as N's, the plural of N for new.
explanation.definitionFit: Carl Nielsen was Denmark's best-known composer, famous for six symphonies.

clue.text: Judge with some land admits that Parisian secured impressive bower

indicators.note: admits means lets in, so one piece holds the others

parts.note: an acre is a measure of land
que is French for that
something lined up has been arranged or secured

explanation.surface: A judge who owns land that has been secured with an impressive garden arbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bower' looks like a garden shelter but means one who bows: a cellist.
explanation.definitionFit: The British cellist was a celebrated player who used a bow, hence an impressive bower.

clue.text: Mobilise forces and get rid of good for nothing

indicators.note: mobilise means set in motion, so these letters move about
to get rid of something is to remove it

explanation.surface: A call to mobilise the armed forces and get rid of anything good-for-nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good for nothing' reads as one phrase but splits: 'good' is the letter lost, 'for nothing' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something given for nothing costs nothing; it is free of charge.

clue.text: New order for 2 half-cuts of meat and 10 eggs to be delivered here?

indicators.note: a new order for something means its letters rearranged

parts.note: a T-bone steak is two half-cuts, sirloin and fillet; two halves make T-bones
X is the Roman numeral ten

explanation.surface: A butcher's order for meat and a box of ten eggs to be delivered.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' and '10' look like references to other clues, but here they are plain numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A box put up for birds to nest in is where eggs are laid, cryptically delivered.

clue.text: Required, once head of Hull, to make every second count

indicators.note: every second letter of the phrase is taken, starting from its second

explanation.surface: A former head of Hull insisting that every second must count.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' looks like part of the definition, an old-fashioned word for required, but its letters are in the phrase read.
explanation.definitionFit: Needful is a slightly dated word for necessary, as in 'do the needful'.

clue.text: Evidence of snoozing in line, military failure

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: a file is a line of soldiers one behind another
ZZ is the cartoon sign of someone snoring

explanation.surface: A soldier dozing in the ranks, a military failure.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that fizzles peters out, ending as a damp squib or flop.

clue.text: Sweet-smelling superior?

parts.note: toffee is a sweet
nosed means sniffed or smelled

explanation.surface: A superior perfume that smells sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: Toffee-nosed is British slang for snobbish and stuck-up, looking down on others.

clue.text: Strings player cancelling her top spot

indicators.note: cancelling means scrubbing out, so these letters vanish

parts.note: a zitherist plays the zither, a stringed instrument
taken as written
1ST, first, is top; written IST

explanation.surface: A musician who cancels his partner's top billing.
explanation.walkthrough: IST stands for 1st, first place, the top.
explanation.definitionFit: A zit is slang for a pimple, a spot on the skin.

clue.text: Outstanding poetry recital

indicators.note: a recital is something spoken out to an audience

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem

explanation.surface: A remarkable poetry reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise for the recital but means unpaid.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt still outstanding is one yet to be paid, still due.

clue.text: The tone of "Oh! How I Hate to Get Up in the Morning"?

definitions.text: The tone of "Oh! How I Hate to Get Up in the Morning"?

parts.words: The tone of "Oh! How I Hate to Get Up in the Morning"?
parts.note: the song is by Irving Berlin and its mood is gloomy; tone also means a colour shade

explanation.walkthrough: Irving Berlin wrote the song in 1918; its downbeat feeling is blue. Berlin blue is another name for the pigment Prussian blue.
explanation.definitionFit: Prussian blue pigment, also named after Berlin, is a tone or shade of colour.
